page.hero_summary: GLP-1TRZ is a supplier catalog name, not a scientific one. Vendors across the research market use it, along with spellings like GLP-1 TRZ and GLP1-TRZ, for material represented as tirzepatide, the 39-residue dual GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist also known by its development code LY3298176. The name itself proves nothing about sequence, salt form, or purity. What proves those things is the paperwork attached to the vial you receive. This page sets out what is established for tirzepatide from regulatory and peer-reviewed sources, what only a lot certificate of analysis can establish, and where the two are routinely confused. Supplied for laboratory research use only, not for human or veterinary use.

sections.heading: Overview
body: Walk the research peptide market and you will meet the same molecule under half a dozen names. GLP-1TRZ, GLP-1 TRZ, GLP1-TRZ, TRZ. None of these appear in PubChem, in FDA labeling, or in the peer-reviewed literature. They are trade shorthand, and they exist largely because suppliers avoid the approved drug names attached to the same active molecule.

The scientific entity behind the shorthand is tirzepatide. It carries the development code LY3298176, CAS 2023788-19-2, and PubChem CID 156588324. Prescribing information from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration describes it as a glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) receptor and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist, built on the GIP sequence.

Here is the part most product pages skip. A supplier label does not carry chemical identity with it. A vial marked GLP-1TRZ is tirzepatide if, and only if, its analytical documentation says so and the report belongs to that lot. Treat the name as a pointer to what the material is meant to be, and treat the COA as the evidence of what it is.

sections.heading: What this material is for
body: This listing supports in vitro and preclinical laboratory work: incretin receptor pharmacology, GIP and GLP-1 signaling assays, comparative studies against single-receptor and triple-receptor peptides, and analytical method development. It is not a drug, supplement, cosmetic, or food, and it is not intended for administration to humans or animals.
Nothing on this page provides dosing, administration, titration, reconstitution for injection, or treatment information, and none should be inferred from the clinical literature discussed below.

sections.heading: Why the molecular weight is printed three different ways
sections.intro: Catalogs quote tirzepatide at 4813.53, 4813.45, and around 4810.52, and researchers reasonably wonder which one is wrong. None of them is. They describe different measurements.

rows: Average molecular weight as stated in FDA prescribing information for the approved product
Average molecular weight from analytical reference standard suppliers, from the same formula
Accurate (monoisotopic) mass, the figure a high-resolution mass spectrometer reports
Analytical reference data and MS reports

sections.outro: The gap between the first two is rounding in atomic mass tables applied to a 225-carbon molecule. The gap to the third is the difference between an averaged isotope distribution and the single lightest isotopologue. A COA that quotes an observed mass without saying which convention it used has left out the information you need to judge it.

sections.heading: What the receptor research shows
body: Tirzepatide engages the receptors for two incretin hormones in one molecule, which is the feature that made it interesting to metabolic researchers. FDA labeling states that it selectively binds and activates both the GIP and GLP-1 receptors, that it enhances first-phase and second-phase insulin secretion, that it reduces glucagon in a glucose-dependent way, and that it delays gastric emptying.

The C20 fatty diacid does the pharmacokinetic work. It drives binding to plasma albumin, reported at 99 percent, which is the reason the molecule persists long enough for weekly dosing in the approved product rather than clearing in minutes.

Receptor engagement is not symmetrical, and that detail matters to anyone designing an assay. A 2020 study in JCI Insight characterized tirzepatide as an imbalanced and biased dual agonist. Occupancy calculations pointed to greater engagement of the GIP receptor than the GLP-1 receptor. At the GIP receptor, signaling resembled native GIP. At the GLP-1 receptor, the molecule favored cAMP generation over beta-arrestin recruitment and drove receptor internalization less strongly than GLP-1 itself.
sections.evidence_classification: In vitro receptor pharmacology and primary islet work for the bias findings, with animal models. Human clinical pharmacology for the insulin, glucagon and gastric emptying statements, all from studies of the approved pharmaceutical product.

sections.heading: Where the human evidence stops
body: Tirzepatide has a large clinical record, built on the SURPASS program in type 2 diabetes and the SURMOUNT program in weight management. That record belongs to a regulated, sterile, formulated injectable made under pharmaceutical manufacturing controls.

It does not transfer to a research powder. A clinical trial result establishes nothing about a research lot's sequence fidelity, purity, aggregation state, endotoxin content, sterility, or excipient profile. Any supplier who points at trial data to imply something about a vial of research material is making a claim the data cannot support, and that includes any vial sold by Veracue.

sections.heading: What a GLP-1TRZ certificate of analysis has to do

sections.heading: HPLC and mass spectrometry answer different questions
body: Vendors tend to list the two side by side as though they were interchangeable proof. They are not.

RP-HPLC separates the target peptide from related substances, truncated and deletion sequences, and other chromatographic impurities. It supports a purity percentage under the stated conditions. It says nothing about what the main peak actually is.

Mass spectrometry measures mass-to-charge behavior and tells you whether the observed mass is consistent with the expected molecule, including the lipidated Lys20 conjugate. It says nothing about how much of the sample is that molecule.

Run together, they are complementary: one supports identity, the other supports purity. Run alone, either leaves a hole. Neither speaks to sterility, endotoxin, residual solvents, water content, or aggregation, so none of those can be inferred from a purity line.

One practical warning. A reported purity above 100 percent is a signal, not a rounding quirk. It usually means an assay or normalization problem, and it is a reason to ask the supplier for the chromatogram and the method rather than to accept the figure.

faq.question: What is GLP-1TRZ?
faq.answer: GLP-1TRZ is a supplier catalog name used across the research peptide market for material represented as tirzepatide, a synthetic dual GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist. It is not a scientific name and does not appear in chemical databases or regulatory labeling. Veracue supplies it as a laboratory research material.

faq.question: Is GLP-1TRZ the same as tirzepatide?
faq.answer: It is meant to be, and the market uses the two names for the same molecule. The name by itself does not prove it. A specific lot is tirzepatide when its analytical documentation supports that identity and the report matches the vial. Ask for the COA rather than relying on the label.

faq.question: What is LY3298176?
faq.answer: LY3298176 is the development code for tirzepatide, used through its clinical program and still common in the scientific literature. Searching that code alongside the name is the quickest way to reach primary sources rather than vendor pages.

faq.question: What is the tirzepatide sequence and how long is it?
faq.answer: Tirzepatide is a 39-amino-acid synthetic peptide based on the native GIP sequence. FDA labeling describes aminoisobutyric acid at positions 2 and 13, a C-terminal amide, and a lysine at position 20 attached to 1,20-eicosanedioic acid through a linker. The full residue-by-residue sequence for a given lot should come from its documentation.

faq.question: What is the molecular weight of tirzepatide?
faq.answer: FDA prescribing information gives 4813.53 Da with the empirical formula C225H348N48O68. Analytical reference suppliers commonly list 4813.45 g/mol from the same formula, and the accurate or monoisotopic mass is around 4810.52 Da. The values differ by convention, not by disagreement.

faq.question: What is the CAS number for tirzepatide?
faq.answer: CAS 2023788-19-2 is the number associated with tirzepatide, and PubChem lists it under CID 156588324. A CAS number attaches to a chemical identity, not to a vial, so it should not be assigned to a lot that has no identity testing behind it.

faq.question: What receptors does tirzepatide act on?
faq.answer: Both the GIP receptor and the GLP-1 receptor. Engagement is not equal across the two. A 2020 JCI Insight study described greater occupancy at the GIP receptor and, at the GLP-1 receptor, signaling biased toward cAMP generation over beta-arrestin recruitment.

faq.question: Why does tirzepatide carry a fatty acid?
faq.answer: The C20 fatty diacid at Lys20 drives binding to plasma albumin, reported at 99 percent in FDA labeling. That association slows clearance. It is also the part of the molecule most worth confirming analytically, since an unconjugated peptide would give a different mass.

faq.question: How is GLP-1TRZ purity tested, and what does the number mean?
faq.answer: Purity is normally reported by reversed-phase HPLC as a percentage of detected peak area under stated conditions. It describes chromatographic purity and nothing else. It does not establish identity, net peptide content, sterility, endotoxin status, or biological activity.

faq.question: What is the difference between HPLC and LC-MS on a COA?
faq.answer: HPLC separates the target from related substances and supports the purity figure. Mass spectrometry compares an observed mass against the expected one and supports identity. One answers how pure, the other answers what it is. A COA that reports only one has answered half the question.

faq.question: Is GLP-1TRZ an approved medicine?
faq.answer: No. Tirzepatide is the active ingredient in approved prescription products, but those are sterile, formulated, regulated drug products made under pharmaceutical controls. A research powder sold under a catalog name is a separate, unapproved material for laboratory use only, and it is not a substitute for any prescription medicine.
